title: Six million
hook: six million Jews were murdered, alongside Roma, disabled people and many others

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janusz Korczak, and your line: he stayed with them. Did you stay a little longer with someone who needed you? Today is a number, the one in the title. We'll take it slowly. Day one thousand fourteen.

A highway in Israel, mid-morning, traffic moving fast. Then a siren starts, long and steady, across the whole country at once. The cars slow and stop, right there in the lanes. Drivers open their doors and step out and stand beside them, heads down. On sidewalks, in shops, in classrooms, people stand still. Nobody speaks. Then the siren fades, and the cars start again. It's Yom HaShoah, the day of remembrance for the Holocaust. Today's word is the number they're standing for.
screen: `A SIREN ACROSS A COUNTRY.` → `DRIVERS STANDING IN THE LANES.` → `NOBODY SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Six million. That is the number of Jews murdered in the Holocaust, as Yad Vashem and historians of the Shoah count them. Men and women, grandparents, babies. Whole families, whole towns, whole ways of life. They were shot at the edges of pits, starved in ghettos, and murdered in camps built to kill. And they were not alone. The Nazis and their collaborators also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, gay men, political prisoners and many others. Remembering one group of the dead never erases another. A number that large is almost impossible to hold. The mind slides off it. Jewish tradition has a way of turning it around. The Mishnah, in a passage about witnesses in a court where a life is at stake, teaches that one human being was created first, alone, so that we would learn this: whoever destroys a single soul is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single soul is as if they saved a whole world. So the title is not one number. It is six million worlds, each one complete. And what do you say in front of that? The Torah tells of Aaron, whose two sons died suddenly in the sanctuary. Moses speaks to him. And Aaron answers with nothing. "And Aaron held his peace." Some readers hear that silence not as an absence of words, but as the only honest answer. Silence is part of how the Holocaust is remembered too, as on that highway when the siren sounds.
screen: `THE JEWISH DEAD OF THE SHOAH.` · `ROMA, DISABLED PEOPLE, AND MANY OTHERS.` · `ONE SOUL, A WHOLE WORLD.` · `AARON'S SILENCE.` · then, large: `AND AARON HELD HIS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: keep one minute of silence, and then a little more. If you can, stand, the way the drivers stand beside their cars. If you'd rather sit, sit. Let your breath slow. Don't try to picture six million. You can't, and you don't have to. Let just one person be in the silence with you, anyone, a child, an old woman, a face from an old photo. One whole world. Then let the silence hold all the others. No words. If you pray, let the silence be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Six million. The Jews murdered in the Holocaust, each one, as the Mishnah teaches, a whole world, remembered alongside the Roma, disabled people and all the others the Nazis killed. Today's word.
Your line: each one a whole world. Today, when you meet one person, let them be a whole world for a moment, the way the Mishnah asks. Day one thousand fourteen.

howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, Israel stops for a siren while people stand in silence, and Jewish communities elsewhere hold memorial services with candles, the reading of names and the memorial prayers.
